title: Developing Effective Approaches to Extend Hematopoietic Healthspan by Targeting Cell-Extrinsic and Cell-Intrinsic Alterations at Middle Age
text:
Aging is a complex process that contributes to reduced function and elevated risk of various diseases in
tissues throughout the body, including the blood system. The impact of aging on human health is of
increasing societal concern due to the worldwide increase in the age of our population. Our research is
relevant to public health because it will provide new information that can be used to develop therapies to
sustain a healthy and robust blood system during aging and reduce risk of diseases such as blood cancer,
cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes.

title: HIGHLY PARALLEL ANALYSIS OF 5' AND 3' UTR VARIANTS IN NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS
text:
A significant fraction of cases of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) are caused by coding mutations that
prematurely terminate the translation of specific RNAs into proteins. However, protein production can also be
disrupted by mutations in the untranslated regions (UTRs) of RNAs. We propose to detect and analyze new
NDD mutations by bringing to bear a unique set of tools specifically designed to study translational regulation
by UTRs, extending the utility of ongoing efforts to sequence the genomes of tens of thousands of NDD cases
across the US and the world.

title: Mechanism and therapeutic potential of microglia regulation in glioblastoma
text:
The project will reveal the underlying molecular mechanisms for how OLFML3 triggers microglial infiltration in
CLOCK/BMAL1-high GBM. Based on these mechanistic results, the project will develop novel therapeutic
strategies targeting microglial infiltration with or without with immune checkpoint inhibitors for GBM.

title: High-throughput optimization of gene editing systems for treating Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal adult-onset neurological disease in which motor
neurons degenerate, thereby leading to paralysis and death due to respiratory failure. There are
no existing therapies that specifically target the repeat expansions in the C9ORF72 gene that are
known to cause ALS. Acrobat Genomics will protein engineer optimized and compact RNA-
guided nucleases to precisely target and deplete repeat-bearing C9ORF72 transcripts as a
potential therapeutic for patients with ALS.

title: Novel targeted therapy for treating Ovarian Cancer
text:
Ovarian Cancer (OCa) is the deadliest of all gynecologic cancers in the United States and a critical need exists
for development of novel therapies treating OCa. With our expertise in developing novel small molecule inhibitors
that disrupt protein-protein interactions, we have rationally designed and synthesized a small chemical molecule
that function as LIFR inhibitor (EC359). The research proposed in this application is clinically significant because
it will establish a mechanism and therapeutic potential of a first-in-class LIFR inhibitor EC359. This inhibitor can
be utilized as a monotherapy, or as a combination therapy using in vitro and in vivo preclinical models; and thus,
create a new paradigm of using LIFR inhibitor as a novel therapy for curbing OCa progression.

title: Mayo Clinic / University of Minnesota Prostate SPORE
text:
The Mayo Clinic–University of Minnesota SPORE in Prostate Cancer (Mayo/UMN Prostate SPORE) is a revised
(A1) application that seeks to decrease the morbidity and mortality associated with prostate cancer by making
transformative scientific advances that address critical questions in prostate cancer biology and treatment
science. The Mayo/UMN Prostate SPORE includes four translational research projects (all of which are
supported by three cores) that together identify and address major barriers and challenges that exist for the
clinical management of advanced castration-resistant prostate cancer. These projects are highly collaborative
in terms of the multidisciplinary expertise of their clinical and basic science co-leaders and with respect to the
collaborative infrastructure and multi-institutional trial leadership which positions the Mayo/UMN Prostate
SPORE as a unique and vital initiative for advancing patient care and scientific discovery.

title: A principled, novel rabies virus toolbox for tracing synaptic circuits and pinpointing how neuronal innate immunity shapes viral spread in the brain
text:
The use of Rabies lyssavirus vectors for understanding the brain’s synaptic organization is limited by our
understanding of the virus’ impact on host-cell innate immunity, a viral strain-specific property that is largely
unexplored. The proposed experiments address this gap by coupling a highly neuroinvasive (yet biosafe)
rabies strain with and without mutations that disinhibit innate immune signaling in neurons with quantitative
analysis of infected neurons molecular properties and viral spreading phenotypes. This study will establish a
cutting-edge viral reagent for neural circuit analysis and will characterize how neuronal innate immune
signaling shapes viral infection properties in vivo, with broad implications for understanding and treating
neurotropic infections.

title: Dissecting the molecular pathways controlling human pacemaker development
text:
This project aims to uncover how the human heart’s natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node (SAN), develops and
functions by identifying the key genes and signals that guide its formation. Using advanced stem cell models,
gene editing tools, and organoids that mimic the pacemaker, we will also study how genetic risk factors linked to
heart rhythm disorders affect SAN development. These insights could lead to new strategies for treating sinus
node dysfunction and other heart conduction diseases.

title: NIAID Virology Quality Assurance (VQA)
text: The purpose of the NIAID Virology Quality Assurance (VQA) program is to provide a comprehensive quality assessment program for virologic assays for HIV and associated viral pathogens performed on samples collected from participants enrolled in NIAID-sponsored and collaborative multisite clinical studies. The goal of the VQA program is to ensure the validity and inter- and intra-laboratory comparability of virologic laboratory data by providing laboratories with proficiency testing (PT) panels and real-time assay run controls and analyzing PT panel and assay run data within each laboratory and across laboratories participating in the program. The VQA program implements standards of performance for new and existing state-of-the-art virologic assays, develops and employs biostatistical methods relating to the assays, and acquires, tests, stores and dispenses quality control materials (QCMs) and reagents. The VQA program is critical to the scientific integrity of on-going and future studies concerning HIV diagnosis, pathogenesis, drug resistance, and cure, including the assessment of vaccine and treatment efficacy, and post-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP).

title: The interplay of parental reward-related neurophysiology and behavior in the intergenerational transmission of positive valence dysfunction in early adolescents
text:
Anhedonia, the pervasive loss of interest and/or pleasure, is a symptom of many forms of serious mental illness
that is highly impairing, resistant to treatment, and particularly likely to emerge among adolescent offspring of
anhedonic parents. This K01 aims to describe neurophysiological and behavioral pathways that contribute to the
transmission of anhedonia within families, examining the role of everyday parenting behaviors in amplifying or
attenuating neurophysiological risks for anhedonia during early adolescence. Findings will advance
understanding of pathways contributing to risk and resilience among vulnerable youth and may inform targets
for prevention efforts to reduce risk for the intergenerational transmission of serious mental illness.

title: Regulating Skeletal Connectivity in Craniofacial Development and Disease
text:
The craniofacial skeleton is composed of diverse tissue types and their precise integration during
development is necessary for normal structure and function. We propose to use mouse and human genetics
to reveal the mechanisms that coordinate development, assembly, and maintenance of the craniofacial
skeleton as multi-tissue system. Our overall goal is to reveal new insights into the etiology of congenital
craniofacial disorders and harness this knowledge for therapeutic innovations.

title: Determinants of toxicity and response to immune checkpoint blockade through integrative profiling of T cell clonal dynamics and plasma cell- free DNA
text:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed modern cancer medicine, however the severe toxicity
rate is up to ~60% in melanoma patients treated with combination immunotherapy. Unfortunately, the
pathophysiology underlying these severe immune-related toxicities remains unclear, and we have no
way in clinical practice to forecast who will experience them. To address these issues, we will perform
multi-modal high-dimensional profiling of melanoma peripheral blood to delineate cellular determinants
of immunotherapy-related toxicities and to devise an assay for predicting both immunotherapy
response and toxicity from pretreatment plasma cell-free DNA using genome-wide methylation
sequencing.

title: Biomolecular Research Core
text: Biomolecular Research Core The Biomolecular Research Core (BRC) of the COBRE in Matrix Biology is dedicated to supporting investigators in mass spectrometry, histology and imaging, characterization of molecular interactions, and design and development of tissue and cell-based models for the study of the ECM in a timely and reliable manner. The BRC was the first biomedical research core facility at Boise State University. It represented an initial step in Boise State’s trajectory to become a research university that makes significant strides in addressing high impact biomedical research issues. Phases 1 and 2 of COBRE support resulted in the growth of the BRC. To foster a sustainable research environment, the BRC is built on strong institutional support and skilled research staff. The BRC has become a critical resource for COBRE investigators and many other investigators across campus. During phase 3, the BRC will provide expertise for planning of experiments, interpretation of research results, and preparation of publication quality figures and tables. Trained staff will be available to provide technical expertise as needed and access to specialized equipment. BRC staff will provide training to new users and early stage investigators as needed. Due to its importance to research infrastructure, the university is committed to providing dedicated space, maintenance of essential equipment, and support for training opportunities for new investigators. Institutional support exists for the Core Director, Associate Core Director, biostatistician, and research technicians. Such support will enable sustainability of the BRC to support biomedical research investigators as we focus on growing the user base both internally and externally. Sustaining the infrastructure within the BRC will meet the needs of investigators and further, will allow expansion of Boise State’s biomedical research capabilities. The BRC will support biomedical research training and education programs for graduate students through formal courses, one-on-one training, and through workshops. A business plan to allow sustainability will be based on a fee-for-service model and adopting best practices of small businesses that apply to share core facilities. Aims for phase 3 include 1) expanding the user base to ensure long-term sustainability and 2) maintaining effective management and operations for the core. The BRC has become a key part of research programs across campus and will continue to provide services to biomedical research investigators beyond phase 3 of the COBRE program.

title: Imaging signatures of early tuberculosis
text:
Detecting and treating tuberculosis (TB) before it becomes infectious or leads to disability is
critical to TB control. We propose to use artificial intelligence combined with digital chest
imaging (computed tomography and chest-X-rays) to develop a high-precision imaging toolset
to characterize and diagnose early TB disease.

title: Strategies to Enhance Engineered Heart Tissue Based Myocardial Repair
text:
Heart regeneration holds great promise to treat ischemic heart diseases, which have long been the leading
cause of death worldwide. The long term goal and the clinical significance of this project are to engineer a
novel human heart tissue with robust myocardial regeneration and repairing potency. The results from these
studies will serve as an important platform to enhance future therapeutic initiatives aimed at heart regeneration.

title: Engineering ingestible nanosensors for breath-based detection of colorectal cancer
text:
Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in the United States, and early
detection is key to reducing the 53,000 deaths per year. To improve early detection, non-invasive
diagnostic tests are needed to improve adherence rates to screening guidelines. To address this
need, we seek to enable breath-based detection of colorectal cancer by developing ingestible
sensors that can detect disease activity in the intestine and release reporters that are exhaled for
non-invasive detection in breath.

title: Biophysical foundations of evolutionary dynamics
text:
Through combination of experimentation and multiscale biophysical modeling this research will provide tools to
predict antibiotic escape and other drug resistance dynamics. It will pave the path to develop new approaches
to counter drug resistance in evolving pathogens.

title: Investigation of epitranscriptomic crosstalks related to autism using real patients and brain organoids
text:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition affecting 1 in 36 U.S. children,
with profound lifelong impacts on individuals, families, and society. This project investigates how environmental
exposures, such as heavy metals (cadmium) and endocrine-disrupting chemicals (PFAS), interact with
protective factors like prenatal folic acid to disrupt RNA modifications and DNA methylation, contributing to ASD
risk. By integrating brain organoid models with multi-omics analyses, this research aims to uncover molecular
mechanisms underlying ASD, identify biomarkers for early detection, and inform precision medicine strategies
to reduce risk and improve outcomes.

title: Directing Membrane Function with Inositol Lipids in Health and Disease
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because many genetic, infectious and neoplastic diseases
are driven by changes in PI(4,5)P2 levels. We seek to identify the basic mechanisms whereby healthy cells
control PI(4,5)P2 levels and couple them to multiple, parallel PI(4,5)P2-dependent membrane functions,
revealing basic cellular mechanisms underpinning these diseases. Therefore, the research is relevant to NIH's
and NIGMS's central mission of seeking fundamental knowledge about living systems and life processes that
lay foundations for advances in disease treatment and prevention.

title: Systematic investigation of artifacts in deep learning-based PET image enhancement
text:
This project investigates how artificial intelligence-based image enhancement tools may unintentionally introduce
false or misleading features into positron emission tomography images. Understanding and predicting the
occurrence of these effects is essential to ensure accurate diagnosis, improve patient safety, and support the
responsible clinical use of deep learning in medical imaging.
